theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What are the "terms of reference" of a technical report?
options: The list of books and websites used to write the report
The page numbers and headings shown on the contents page
The names and job titles of everyone who reads the report
What the report must cover, for whom, and by when

questions.stem: The same weld failure must be reported to the works manager, who is short of time, and to the welding team. What is the best approach?
options: Start with a short summary, and keep the detail in the body
Write only the technical detail, since the manager can ask
Write only a one-line note, since the welders saw the failure
Write two reports with different facts for each of the readers

questions.stem: The manager asks whether the Centre should buy a plasma cutter or keep using oxy-fuel for thin sheet. Which kind of report fits this request?
options: An incident report
A weekly progress report
A recommendation report
A machine test record

questions.stem: Before repairs are priced, which report records the state of an existing steel staircase, defect by defect?
options: A job completion report
A condition survey report
A weekly time sheet
A material order form

questions.stem: Before collecting data for a report on weld rejects, what should you decide first?
options: Which font, colours and logo the report will use
Who in the team will be blamed for the rejects
How many pages long the finished report must be
The question it must answer and the data needed

questions.stem: Why does a test report include a section that describes the method used?
options: So someone else could repeat the test and check the results
So the report is long enough to look like serious work
So the reader does not need to look at the results at all
So the tester can show that he owns the test equipment

questions.stem: What is the difference between a conclusion and a recommendation in a report?
options: A conclusion comes first; a recommendation is only a summary
A conclusion is an opinion; a recommendation is a measured fact
A conclusion says what findings mean; a recommendation, what to do
There is no difference; the two words mean the same thing

questions.stem: Of 30 welds made with electrodes left out overnight, 12 were porous. Of 30 made with electrodes from the oven, 1 was porous. Which conclusion does this data support?
options: All the welders need to be retrained at once
Damp electrodes are the likely main cause
The welding machines are worn out and must go
Porosity cannot be avoided in this workshop

questions.stem: Which recommendation is written best?
options: Electrodes should be looked after better by everyone from now on
Someone should probably think about the electrode problem soon
Electrode storage needs to be improved as much as possible
Storeman to keep low-hydrogen electrodes in the oven, from 1 June

questions.stem: Why is the summary of a long report usually written last?
options: It can only sum up the findings once they are all written
It is the least important part, so it can wait until the end
It must repeat the whole report word for word
The reader never reads it, so time is better spent elsewhere

questions.stem: The body of a report discusses only the average and the highest of 40 hardness readings. Where should the full table of readings go?
options: Nowhere: once averaged, the readings can be thrown away
In the summary, so the manager sees every reading first
In an appendix, referred to from the text
In the title, so the reader knows what the report is about

questions.stem: Which is best for showing how the weekly reject rate changed over six months?
options: A pie chart
A line graph
A photograph
A list of names

questions.stem: Which is best for comparing the number of each type of defect (porosity, undercut, slag, cracks) found this month?
options: A line graph joining the defect types
A sketch of one of the welds
A paragraph listing each defect once
A bar chart

questions.stem: Why must every graph in a report have a title and axes labelled with their units?
options: So the reader knows what is plotted and how it was measured
So the graph fills the page and looks more professional
So the printer can find the graph when printing the report
So nobody needs to read the text that explains the graph

questions.stem: A thickness gauge reads to 0.1 mm. How should a reading from it be written in a report?
options: To 0.001 mm, such as 9.700 mm
To the nearest 10 mm, such as 10 mm
To 0.1 mm, such as 9.7 mm
In words, such as "just under ten"

questions.stem: A draft report gives the average leg length as 6.2 mm, but the spreadsheet of readings shows 6.8 mm. What should you do?
options: Use 6.5 mm, the value halfway between the two
Find which is right, correct it and note the change
Leave it, as a difference of 0.6 mm is very small
Delete the average so that nobody can question it

questions.stem: Which sentence is best for the findings section of an inspection report?
options: The welder was careless and this weld is a disaster.
Weld W4 looks a bit dodgy near the far end of it.
I think there might be something wrong with W4.
W4: 25 mm crack at the toe, found by dye penetrant.

questions.stem: A friend of yours made the faulty weld you are reporting on. How should this affect your report?
options: Not at all: report the facts as you would for anyone
Leave the weld out of the report to protect your friend
Blame the electrodes so that your friend is not named
Report it, but make the fault sound smaller than it is

questions.stem: A failure report says only: "Cause of failure: weld cracked." Why is this not enough?
options: It is too short to fill the space on the report form
It should name the person who made the weld instead
It says what happened, but not why the weld cracked
Cracks should never be mentioned in a written report

questions.stem: Why should a photo of a weld defect include a rule or scale and a label showing where it is?
options: So the photo looks neat and tidy and fills the frame well
So the reader can judge its size and find it on the job
So the camera can focus properly on the weld
So the photo can be used again on another job

questions.stem: A report has 12 photos. What is the best way to refer to them in the text?
options: Put them all at the end without any numbers or captions
Describe each one as "the photo above" or "the photo below"
Send them separately by phone so the report stays short
Number them, and refer to each one by its number

questions.stem: In a weld inspection report, why is each weld's number and the welder's identification recorded?
options: So each result can be traced to the weld and its welder
So the welder who made the most welds can be paid a bonus
So the inspector can finish writing the report more quickly
So the client knows the names of all the staff

questions.stem: Your report says that a weld is not acceptable. What should it state to back this up?
options: How you felt when you first saw the weld
How many years the welder has worked at the company
The limit it breaks and the document that sets it
That other inspectors agree with your opinion

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the active voice, which is usually the clearest way to write a report?
options: The liner replacement was effected by the team in due course.
The team replaced the torch liner on 3 March.
Replacement of the liner was carried out at some point.
It was decided that the liner was to be replaced by us.

questions.stem: Why should one term be used for one thing all through a report, for example always "fillet weld" and never sometimes "corner weld"?
options: Because long words make the report look more expert
Because the spell checker only knows one of the words
Because the client will pay less for a report with new words
Because the reader may think a new word means a new thing

questions.stem: A long report uses many abbreviations, such as WPS, NDT, HAZ and PPE. What helps the reader most?
options: A list of the abbreviations and their meanings near the front
Using as many abbreviations as possible to save space
Changing the abbreviations on each page to keep it interesting
Leaving them, because every reader should know them already

questions.stem: Which is the clearest way to write the range of leg lengths measured on a weld?
options: about 6 mm or a bit more
6.0 mm to 6.8 mm
6 to 6.8mm-ish

questions.stem: A report gives a reject rate as a percentage. What should be shown with it?
options: A note that percentages are always rounded up
The numbers behind it, such as 6 of 80 welds
The name of the calculator that was used
A second percentage, worked out a different way

questions.stem: Why does a report form have boxes for "checked by" and "approved by" as well as "prepared by"?
options: So that three people share the blame for any mistake
So the report takes longer and seems more important
So the writer does not need to check his own work
To show it was reviewed and accepted before issue

questions.stem: A report was sent to a client as Issue 1. A mistake is then found in it. What should be done?
options: Send a corrected Issue 2 that says what was changed
Phone the client and ask her to change her own copy
Leave it, because the report has already been sent
Send a new copy, also marked Issue 1, without comment

questions.stem: Who should receive a copy of an incident investigation report?
options: Everyone in the company, through the group chat
Only the person who was hurt in the incident
The people named on the report's circulation list
Anyone who asks for a copy, inside or outside

questions.stem: Why must an incident investigation report be accurate, even in small details?
options: Small details make the report longer and look more serious
It may be used later by insurers, inspectors or a court
The injured person will mark it like a school test
Small mistakes can be fixed later in the next report

questions.stem: An investigation finds that a trainee was burned because no screens were set up around a welding job. Which recommendation deals with the root cause?
options: Tell the trainee who was burned to be more careful
Buy a bigger first-aid kit for the welding bay
Put up a poster in the bay saying "Work safely"
Add screens to the pre-start checklist and check daily

questions.stem: When should a non-conformance report be raised?
options: As soon as work is found not to meet the specification
Only when the client complains about the finished job later
At the end of the year, covering every fault found that year
Only if the faulty item has already left the workshop gate

questions.stem: What must a test report give beside each result, so that the reader can tell whether it passed?
options: The time of day that each test was carried out
The price of the test piece and its material
The acceptance limit from the specification
A comment on how well the tester felt it went

questions.stem: A weekly progress report shows that the job is three days behind. What else should it include?
options: Who is to blame, and what has been done to them
The cause, the effect on the finish date and the plan
A promise that the time will be made up somehow
Nothing more, as the dates speak for themselves

questions.stem: Why is a spreadsheet useful when writing a report on 200 thickness readings?
options: It makes up any readings that are missing
It writes the conclusions and recommendations
It removes the need to check the readings at all
It sorts the data, finds averages and draws graphs

questions.stem: Which file name is best for a digital report?
options: J2417_Weld-Inspection_Issue2.pdf
report final final NEW.pdf
scan0001.pdf
Ricardo report.docx

questions.stem: On a survey of rusted balcony rails at a hotel in Negril, what should be recorded for each defect?
options: Only the defects that can be seen from the ground floor
The guest's room number and the date of their stay
Its location, size, photo number and how serious it is
A general comment that the rails are in poor condition

questions.stem: A survey report lists 15 repairs. How should the recommendations be set out?
options: In the order the defects were found on the walk round
In order of priority, with urgent safety items first
In alphabetical order of the parts of the structure
In order of cost, with the cheapest repairs first

questions.stem: A trainee's draft inspection report mixes facts and opinions in the findings. What is the best feedback?
options: Tell him the report is poor and write it yourself
Sign it anyway, as the facts are in there somewhere
Tell him to remove every sentence with an adjective
Show which lines are opinions and how to state facts

questions.stem: What is a good way to check the numbers in a report before it is issued?
options: Re-add totals and check figures against the records
Read the report quickly once, looking for typing errors
Ask the client to check the numbers after it is sent
Round every number so that small errors do not show

questions.stem: The works manager has two minutes to read your 12-page report. Which parts will she most likely read?
options: The method and the appendices
The contents page and the references
The summary and the recommendations
The title page and the page numbers

questions.stem: How long should the weld inspection reports for a building job be kept?
options: Until the welder who made the welds leaves the company
For the time set by the contract, company or the law
Only until the client has paid the final invoice
One week, then they can be thrown away to save space

questions.stem: Your manager asks you to remove a failed test result from a report because the client "won't understand it". What should you do?
options: Remove it, since the manager is responsible for the report
Remove it, but keep a private copy in case of trouble
Change the result to a pass so the question does not arise
Keep it, explain it clearly and raise your concern

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name of the page at the front of a long report that lists its sections with their page numbers?
What type of graph uses dots for pairs of values, such as heat input against hardness, to show whether they are linked?
What is the name of the section that lists the documents and standards used in writing a report?
What is the name of the list in a report that explains the special words and trade terms it uses?
What is the name of the part of a non-conformance report that says what will be done with the faulty item, such as repair, use as is, or scrap?
What is the word for the short description written under a photo or a figure in a report?
What do we call the list of people who must receive a copy of a report?
What one word describes a report that keeps to the facts and is not swayed by personal feelings?
What do we call the first full version of a report, written so that it can be checked before it is issued?
A summary written at the front of a report for busy managers is often called the ______ summary. What is the missing word?
What type of chart shows the parts of a whole as slices of a circle?
What is the name of the section in which the writer explains what the results mean, before giving the conclusions?
What do we call data made of measured or counted numbers, such as readings and totals, rather than descriptions?
What is the name of the horizontal axis of a graph?
What word names the ability to link a finished part back to its material, its welder and its inspection records?

essays.stem: The principal of a school in Spanish Town asks your company to inspect the welded handrails on two staircases and report on their condition. Explain how you would plan, write and issue the report.
essays.modelAnswer: First I agree the terms of reference with the principal: what is to be inspected, what she needs to know (for example whether the rails are safe and what repairs are needed), and by when. I plan the inspection and prepare a record sheet, gauges, a tape, a camera and a marker to number each section of rail. On site I inspect each section, record the defects with their location and size, and take photos with a rule in the frame. Back at the office I check my notes and sort the findings. I write the report in a clear order: title page, a short summary, an introduction with the terms of reference, the method, the findings in a table with photo numbers, a conclusion on the condition of each staircase, and recommendations in order of priority. I check every figure against my notes and ask a colleague to review it. It is then approved, given an issue number, sent to the principal and filed.
markingPoints: Agrees the terms of reference (scope, reader's needs, date)
Plans the inspection and the records, and gathers evidence on site (locations, sizes, photos with scale)
Sets out the report in a clear structure with findings in a table
Gives conclusions and prioritised recommendations
Checks the figures, has it reviewed and approved, issues it with a number and files it

essays.stem: Describe the main sections of a full technical report, from the title page to the appendices, and explain why this order helps the reader.
essays.modelAnswer: The title page gives the title, the report number and issue, the date, who it is for and who wrote, checked and approved it. The summary gives the purpose, the main findings and the main recommendations in a few lines. The contents page lists the sections. The introduction states the terms of reference and the background. The method explains how the information was gathered, so that the work could be repeated. The findings or results give the facts and measurements, often in tables and graphs. The discussion explains what the results mean and why they may have happened. The conclusions sum up what the findings show, and the recommendations say what should be done, by whom and when. References list the documents used, and appendices hold the full data and forms. This order helps because a busy reader can get the answer from the summary, while a technical reader can follow the evidence step by step and check how the conclusions were reached.
markingPoints: Title page and summary described correctly
Introduction (terms of reference) and method described correctly
Findings and discussion described correctly
Conclusions, recommendations, references and appendices described correctly
Explains why the order helps both busy and technical readers

essays.stem: In one month the inspection team found these weld defects: porosity 14, undercut 6, slag inclusions 4, cracks 1. Explain how you would present this data in a report and what conclusions and recommendations you could draw from it.
essays.modelAnswer: There are 25 defects in total. I would put the figures in a small table with the defect type, the number and the percentage of the total: porosity 56%, undercut 24%, slag 16% and cracks 4%. To compare the types I would use a bar chart, with the defect types along the horizontal axis and the number on the vertical axis, a title and labelled axes. The table and chart would be numbered and referred to in the text. My conclusion would be that porosity is by far the biggest problem, so it is where the team should look first. Porosity is often caused by damp electrodes, poor gas cover, dirty plate or draughts, so I would recommend checking electrode storage, gas flow and plate cleaning, and recording which welders and machines the porous welds came from. Even though there is only one crack, it must be reported and investigated, because a crack is the most serious defect. I would also recommend comparing next month's figures.
markingPoints: Works out the total (25) and percentages correctly
Uses a table and a bar chart, with title, labelled axes and numbering
Concludes that porosity is the main problem
Recommends sensible checks on the likely causes of porosity
Says the single crack must still be investigated; recommends tracking the trend

essays.stem: A trainee cut his hand when an angle grinder kicked back. Explain how you would investigate and write an incident investigation report that finds the root cause and gives useful recommendations.
essays.modelAnswer: First the injured trainee gets first aid and the scene is made safe, but left as it was if possible. As soon as I can, I gather the facts: I photograph the scene, the grinder, the disc and the guard, and take short written statements from the trainee and any witnesses in their own words. I check records such as the tool inspection tag and the trainee's training record. In the report I give the date, time and place, the people involved, the injury and the first aid given, then the sequence of events. To find the root cause I keep asking why: the grinder kicked back because the disc jammed; it jammed because the work was not clamped; it was not clamped because no vice was free and the risk was not briefed. The recommendations target those causes, for example a second vice, clamping added to the job briefing, and guard and disc checks before use, each with a person and a date. The report is factual, signed and sent to the people on the circulation list.
markingPoints: First aid and scene made safe; evidence preserved
Gathers facts: photos, statements in their own words, tool and training records
Reports date, time, place, people, injury, first aid and sequence of events
Finds the root cause by asking why repeatedly
Recommendations target the root cause, each with a person and date; factual, signed and distributed

essays.stem: Explain how you make sure a technical report is objective and accurate, and what you would do if you were pressured to change its findings.
essays.modelAnswer: A report is objective when it is based on facts that someone else could check. I record what I see and measure at the time, with units, using instruments that are in good condition. I write findings as facts, such as "crack 25 mm long at the toe of weld W4", not as opinions like "bad weld". I keep findings apart from my interpretation, which goes in the discussion, and I say when something is uncertain. I do not leave out results that are unwelcome, and I treat everyone the same, whether or not I know them. I check every figure against the original record and ask someone else to review the draft. If I am pressured to change or remove a finding, I explain politely why the facts must stay, because reports may be used by clients, insurers or a court, and a false report could put people at risk. If the pressure continues, I raise it with a more senior person and keep my original records.
markingPoints: Records facts and measurements at the time, with units and good instruments
Writes findings as facts, separate from opinions and interpretation; states uncertainty
Includes all results, unwelcome ones too, and treats everyone the same
Checks figures against records and has the draft reviewed
Under pressure: keeps the facts, explains why, escalates and keeps original records

essays.stem: During inspection, your team finds that six steel gates have gaps between the gate and the post that are bigger than the drawing allows. Explain how you would write a non-conformance report and see it through to close-out.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first mark the six gates and keep them apart so they are not sent out. Then I raise a non-conformance report with a number. It states the job number, the drawing and its revision, the gates affected and what the requirement is, for example a gap of 10 mm ± 2 mm. It gives what was found: the measured gap on each gate, with photos showing the tape. I state who found it and when. Next the cause is investigated, for example a wrong size on the cut list or a jig set wrongly, and recorded. The disposition is agreed with the person who has authority, such as the supervisor or the client's engineer: repair the gates, use them as they are with a written concession, or scrap them. The action to stop it happening again is also recorded, such as correcting the cut list. After the repair, the gates are inspected again and the results recorded. When everything is complete, the report is signed off as closed and filed with the job.
markingPoints: Marks and separates the faulty gates
Raises a numbered NCR stating the requirement, the measured findings and photos
Investigates and records the cause
Disposition agreed by someone with authority (repair, use as is with concession, scrap); action to prevent it again
Re-inspects, records results, signs off as closed and files the report

essays.stem: Explain how to write clear, useful recommendations in a report, and give three examples for a survey that found rust on the steel balcony rails of a guest house in Ocho Rios.
essays.modelAnswer: Each recommendation should come from the findings and deal with the cause where possible. It should be specific about what is to be done and where, say who should do it and by when, and be possible within the client's means. Recommendations should be numbered and set out in order of priority, with anything affecting safety first, so the reader can act on them and check them later. Vague wording such as "improve the rails" should be avoided. Examples: 1. Close balcony 3 now and fit a temporary barrier, because the bottom rail has rusted through at two posts; the guest house manager, today. 2. Cut out and replace the rusted bottom rails and post bases on balconies 1 to 4, with welds ground and primed; the contractor, within four weeks. 3. Clean back, prime and repaint all the rails with a paint system suited to a sea-air site, and inspect them every six months; the contractor and the guest house manager.
markingPoints: Recommendations follow from the findings and tackle causes
Each is specific: what, where, who and by when
Numbered and in order of priority, with safety first
Avoids vague wording
Gives three sensible, specific examples for the rusted rails

essays.stem: Explain how technical reports should be checked, approved, issued, corrected and stored in a fabrication company.
essays.modelAnswer: The writer first checks his own draft: the facts and figures against the original records, the units, the spelling of technical terms, and that every table, photo and appendix is numbered and referred to. Another competent person then checks it and signs the "checked by" box, and the person with authority, such as the manager, approves it. Each report has a unique number, an issue number and a date. It is sent to the people on the distribution list, usually as a PDF so that it cannot easily be changed, and the date it was sent is recorded. If a mistake is found after issue, the report is not changed quietly: a new issue is made, with a note of what changed, and sent to the same people, and the old issue is marked superseded. Signed originals and the records behind them are stored in the job file and in a backed-up digital folder, kept secure, and held for the time set by the contract, the company or the law.
markingPoints: Writer checks facts, figures, units and references to tables and photos
A second person checks and an authorised person approves
Unique number, issue and date; sent to the distribution list, usually as a PDF
Mistakes corrected by a new issue with a note of changes; old issue marked superseded
Stored securely (paper and backed-up digital) for the required time

essays.stem: Your team is building a steel canopy for a shop in May Pen and is now four days behind the plan. Describe what your weekly progress report to the manager should contain and how you would set it out.
essays.modelAnswer: The report should be short and set out under headings so the manager can see the position quickly. It starts with the job name and number, the week and who wrote it. A one-paragraph summary says that the job is four days behind and gives the new expected finish date. Next comes the progress against the plan: what was planned this week, what was done, and the percentage of the whole job complete, perhaps in a small table or a marked-up bar chart. Then the reasons for the delay, stated as facts: for example, the steel delivery came three days late and one day was lost to rain on site. Then the effect: the new finish date, any extra cost, and any effect on the client or other trades. Then the actions planned to recover time, such as overtime on Saturday or extra help for the painting, and any decisions needed from the manager, such as approving overtime or telling the client. It ends with next week's plan and is signed and dated.
markingPoints: Job details and a short summary with the delay and new finish date
Progress against the plan (done, planned, percentage), perhaps in a table or chart
Reasons for the delay stated as facts
Effect on date, cost and others, and the recovery actions
Decisions needed from the manager, next week's plan; signed and dated

essays.stem: A welded handrail failed when someone leaned on it. Explain how you would change the way you report this failure for three different readers: the client, the works manager and the welding team.
essays.modelAnswer: The facts must be the same for every reader, but the detail, words and focus change. For the client, I would write a short, polite letter or report in plain words. It says what happened, that the area has been made safe, what we found in simple terms, what we will do to put it right and when, and who to contact. I would avoid trade terms or explain them. For the works manager, I would give a full technical report with a summary first: the findings with measurements and photos, the likely cause, the cost and time to repair, the risk to other jobs with similar rails, and recommendations that need her decision. For the welding team, I would brief them at the work area and give a short written note: what failed, for example lack of fusion at the post weld, why it happened, and the exact change to the method, with photos or a sketch. In each case I would check that the reader has understood and can act on it.
markingPoints: Facts stay the same; detail, words and focus change with the reader
Client: short, plain, safety and remedy, timing and contact
Manager: full technical report with summary, cause, cost, risk to other jobs and decisions needed
Welding team: practical briefing on what failed, why and the method change
Checks each reader has understood and can act

practical1.title: Inspect a set of welded samples and write a weld inspection report with a table and a chart
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group 8–10 welded samples (fillet and butt welds) with a mix of good welds and visible defects, a short specification with acceptance limits, and an inspection record sheet. As a group: (1) agree the terms of reference and plan who inspects which samples; (2) number each sample and weld, inspect them with gauges and a magnifier, and record every reading with units; (3) photograph each defect with a rule in the frame and a label showing the weld number; (4) put the results in a table and draw a bar chart of the defect types; (5) write the report together, with a title page, summary, method, findings, conclusions and recommendations, with each member writing one section and checking another member's section; (6) check the figures against the record sheets, sign the "prepared", "checked" and "approved" boxes as the assessor directs, and hand it in as Issue 1. The report may be written by hand or typed on the Centre's computers. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: 8–10 welded samples with a mix of good and defective welds
Specification sheet with visual acceptance limits
Fillet weld gauge, undercut or bridge cam gauge, steel rule, magnifier and torch
Inspection record sheets, paint marker or labels for numbering
Phone or camera for photos; graph paper or a computer with spreadsheet and word processing software
Report template with title page and approval boxes
photos: The samples laid out and numbered
A gauge in use on a weld, with the reading visible
A defect photographed with a rule and its weld label
The results table and bar chart
checklist: Helped agree the terms of reference and the plan
Inspected their samples correctly and recorded readings with units
Took clear defect photos with a scale and a label
Helped build an accurate table and a correctly labelled chart
Wrote one section in clear, factual language
Checked another member's section and corrected errors
Conclusions and recommendations follow from the findings
safety: Wear safety glasses and gloves when handling samples: cut edges can be sharp
Do not grind or change the samples; inspect them as they are
Keep samples on the bench, not on the floor, to avoid trips and dropped steel
Follow the Centre's rules for the computer room if reports are typed

practical2.title: Condition survey of steel items at the Centre and a recommendation report with priorities
practical2.brief: The assessor chooses three or four steel items at the Centre that can be inspected safely from the ground, such as a gate, a stair handrail, a storage rack and a security grill, and gives the group a survey sheet. As a group: (1) agree the terms of reference with the assessor (what to survey, for whom, and by when) and share the items out; (2) survey each item, recording each defect (for example rust, a cracked or broken weld, a loose fixing, a missing part or damaged paint) with its exact location, its size and a photo number; (3) take each photo with a rule or object for scale and a label; (4) make a simple dimensioned sketch of one item showing where its defects are; (5) write a recommendation report with a summary, a findings table, conclusions and numbered recommendations in order of priority, each with who should act and by when; (6) present the top three recommendations to the assessor in five minutes. Every member surveys at least one item, writes one part of the report and presents one recommendation. Do not climb, lift or dismantle anything during the survey. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Tape measure, steel rule, torch and paint marker or labels
Sketch paper, pencils and a straight edge
Report template, or a computer with word processing software
photos: Each item being surveyed, with its label
A defect photographed with a scale
The dimensioned sketch with the defects marked
The findings table and the prioritised recommendations
The group presenting its top three recommendations
checklist: Recorded each defect with its location, size and photo number
Took clear photos with a scale and a label
Contributed accurately to the sketch or the findings table
Wrote recommendations that are specific, with who and when
Put safety items first in the order of priority
Presented a recommendation clearly and answered a question on it
Kept to safe practice during the survey
safety: Survey from the ground only; do not climb on racks, gates or rails
Do not lean on or test a rail or fixing that looks damaged; report it to the assessor at once
Wear gloves when touching rusted or sharp steel
Stay clear of moving gates, vehicles and work going on in the area
